saved_articles.title: American marine biologist gunned down in Negros Oriental, partner assaulted | ABS-CBN News
saved_articles.description: American marine biologist Dr. Kent Carpenter was gunned down inside his residence in Barangay Ajong, Sibulan, Negros Oriental on Sunday night.
saved_articles.text: American marine biologist Dr. Kent Carpenter was gunned down inside his residence in Barangay Ajong, Sibulan, Negros Oriental on Sunday night. Courtesy: Protect the Verde Island Passage/FB via Annie Perez MANILA (UPDATE) — An American marine biologist was gunned down inside his residence in Barangay Ajong, Sibulan, Negros Oriental on Sunday night. The victim was identified as 73-year-old Dr. Kent Carpenter. According to the Sibulan Police Station, the victim was watching television with a 34-year-old Filipina companion when three unidentified individuals wearing bonnets forcibly entered their house, said Capt. Mary Jean Gutierrez, chief of the Sibulan PNP. The victim was shot in the head, killing him instantly. Carpenter was also robbed after he was killed. Speaking to reporters in an online interview, Police Capt. Stephen Polinar, spokesperson of the Negros Oriental Police, said that things were in disarray when investigators arrived. The female companion was also sexually assaulted by the three perpetrators who were wearing bonnets. “They forcefully entered the house, was shot, assaulted the female and then robbed their things,” said Polinar in Cebuano. Carpenter was the author of the landmark scientific paper which declared the Verde Island Passage as the "Center of Marine Shore Fish Biodiversity" in the world. He was also an adjunct professor and associate researcher at Silliman University. All aspects to the victim’s work and personal life are included in the investigation as a special task group is now formed. “We are yet to establish assumptions and presumptions,” added Polinar. Several netizens shared that Carpenter had greatly helped the Philippine marine science community. “We lost a titan,” one netizen shared. “Today is a painful day for the Marine Science Community. Justice for Kent Carpenter,” read another post. A hot pursuit operation is now underway to locate the perpetrators, along with a deeper investigation into the motive behind the crime. PERSON OF INTEREST The Philippine National Police (PNP) has created a Special Investigation Task Group to fast-track the investigation into the Carpenter’s shooting. According to the Police Regional Office–Negros Island Region (PRO-NIR), the SITG is composed of investigators and specialized police units tasked with case buildup, intelligence gathering, forensic evidence processing, and operations aimed at identifying and arresting those responsible. PNP Public Information Office chief PCol. Allen Rae Co said authorities had identified a person of interest in the case. “As of now, meron na po silang person of interest but it is still too early to tell. They are just validating ‘yung mga information na natatatanggap nila,” Co said. Authorities are also conducting forensic examinations, reviewing possible CCTV footage, interviewing witnesses, validating intelligence reports, and reconstructing the suspects' movements before and after the attack. Police said all possible motives remained under investigation. While robbery is among the angles being considered after several belongings were reportedly taken from the house, investigators are also looking into whether the attack could be linked to Carpenter's work or personal life. “We will check all angles, titingnan po natin lahat ng puwedeng motive talaga. It could have been done to mislead ‘yung investigation… It could be connected doon sa kanyang trabaho, sa personal life, puwedeng sa business,” Co said. RELATED VIDEO:

saved_articles.title: American marine biologist shot dead in Negros Oriental home
saved_articles.description: An American marine biologist was shot dead after three unidentified men forcibly entered his home in Sibulan, Negros Oriental late Sunday night, police said.
saved_articles.text:
An American marine biologist was shot dead after three unidentified men forcibly entered his home in Sibulan, Negros Oriental late Sunday night, police said.

In a report by Mark Makalalad on Super Radyo dzBB, the victim was identified as Kent Edward Carpenter, 73, who was reportedly watching television in the living room of his house with his Filipino companion when the men barged in at around 11:30 p.m.

Initial police investigation revealed that one of the assailants shot Carpenter in the head before the three fled the scene.

The victim's 34-year-old companion was also injured during the incident and is undergoing medical and forensic examination.

Authorities have yet to determine the motive behind the attack and are pursuing all possible leads.

The Police Regional Office–Negros Island Region (PRO-NIR) has since activated Special Investigation Task Group (SITG) Carpenter to expedite the investigation.

According to PRO-NIR, investigators are conducting forensic examination, reviewing possible CCTV footage, interviewing witnesses, validating intelligence information, and reconstructing the perpetrators' movements before and after the shooting.

Police are also coordinating with other law enforcement units and partner agencies to identify and arrest the suspects.

"We strongly condemn this senseless act of violence. I have directed our investigators to exhaust all legal means to identify and apprehend those responsible at the soonest possible time," PRO-NIR Regional Director Brigadier General Romano Cardiño said.

"We assure the victim's family, the community, and our foreign visitors that this case is being treated with utmost urgency, and no effort will be spared until justice is served," he added.

Anyone with information about the incident is urged to coordinate with the nearest police station or the Sibulan Municipal Police Station. — VDV GMA News

saved_articles.title: American marine biologist shot dead in Negros Oriental
saved_articles.description: An American marine biologist whose research crowned the Philippines as the center of global marine biodiversity was shot dead inside his home in Negros Oriental on Sunday night, July 12.
saved_articles.text: MANILA, Philippines — An American marine biologist whose research crowned the Philippines as the center of global marine biodiversity was shot dead inside his home in Negros Oriental on Sunday night, July 12. Local reports identified the victim as Kent Carpenter, a 73-year-old American national and adjunct professor at Silliman University's Institute of Environmental and Marine Sciences in Dumaguete City. Three unidentified men forcibly entered Carpenter's residence in Barangay Ajong, Sibulan town, at around 11:30 p.m. on Sunday while he and his 34-year-old Filipino companion were watching television, the Police Regional Office Negros Island Region (PRO NIR) said in a statement Tuesday. One of the men, armed with a handgun, shot the American national in the head, killing him. His companion was also hurt and is undergoing medical and forensic examination, police said. The suspects remain at large and police in their initial report have not established a motive. Regional police said Tuesday morning, July 14, that it has activated a special investigation task group to help arrest the perpetrators and get to the bottom of the case. Investigators are currently "conducting backtracking and forward tracking operations, including the review of possible CCTV footage, witness interviews, intelligence validation, and reconstruction of the suspects’ movements before and after the incident," the statement by the regional police read. “We strongly condemn this senseless act of violence. I have directed our investigators to exhaust all legal means to identify and apprehend those responsible at the soonest possible time," Regional Director PBGen. Romano Cardiño said, as quoted in the statement. "We assure the victim’s family, the community, and our foreign visitors that this case is being treated with utmost urgency, and no effort will be spared until justice is served," he added. Philstar.com has reached out to the US Embassy in Manila for comment. Carpenter was a highly distinguished ichthyologist (zoologist who studies fish) who made several contributions to marine conservation in the world. But his special interest was the Philippines, having studied Philippine marine fishes for over 50 years since 1975. He co-authored the 2005 study that identified the Verde Island Passage as the "center of marine shore fish biodiversity," a finding that boosted the Philippines' standing in global marine science. Recently, the American national was among those who advocated for the designation of the Verde Island Passage as a World Heritage Site. His death has drawn an outpouring of grief and calls for justice from Filipino scientists and conservation groups. Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park and World Heritage Site said in a social media post: "Since 2018, Kent gave his time freely to the park, driven by a love for the reef. He was a brilliant scientist who helped us truly understand what we are protecting." Philstar.com is one of the most vibrant, opinionated, discerning communities of readers on cyberspace. saved_articles.title: Partner of slain US marine biologist now among 'persons of interest' | ABS-CBN News
saved_articles.description: The live-in partner of American marine biologist Dr. Kent Carpenter is now a person of interest in his killing, Negros Oriental Police said Wednesday.
saved_articles.text: Dr. Kent Carpenter, 73, was shot and killed on Sunday night by three unidentified armed men who entered his residence in Barangay Ajong, Sibulan, Negros Oriental. Contributed via Annie Perez MANILA (UPDATE) — The live-in partner of slain American marine biologist Dr. Kent Carpenter has been identified as one of the persons of interest (POIs) in the investigation into his killing, the Negros Oriental Police said Wednesday. Carpenter was shot dead inside his home in Sibulan, Negros Oriental on Sunday evening. American marine biologist gunned down in Negros Oriental His live-in partner survived the attack after sustaining wounds. Negros Oriental Police director Col. Timmar Alam said investigators are closely looking into the woman's account of the incident, noting inconsistencies that surfaced during the investigation. “Unang-una, hindi naman siya sinaktan. At taga doon din siya, lokal din siya na resident doon,” Alam said. Alam said the woman had also claimed she was sexually assaulted by the suspects after being tied up with a charger cord. Scientific community grieves, demands justice for slain marine expert Kent Carpenter However, a vaginal swab examination yielded negative results. “Doon sa claim niya na sinasabi niyang ginapos muna siya ng charger cord, tapos pinadapa siya. Kini-claim niya na she was sexually assaulted, it is still under investigation kasi wala pa po nag-prove,” Alam said. Police are examining why the woman was spared during the attack. “Hindi natin masabi na siya ay involved. Basta sa ngayon, since she was left alive, probably baka kilala or kakilala siya, kilala siya ng mga suspects. We are considering those angles,” Alam said. The police official said the woman told investigators that she and Carpenter had been living together for about seven years. NO FORCED ENTRY Investigators also corrected an earlier report that suggested there had been a forcible entry into the victims' home. Following a more thorough crime scene examination, police found no signs of forced entry. “When we conducted the ocular inspection, wala kami nakikitang forcible entry sa bahay. But meron kami nakitang part sa bahay na pwedeng maakyat, ‘yung parang terrace nila sa taas,” Alam said. Aside from Carpenter's live-in partner, her sibling has also been listed as a person of interest because of his frequent visits to the house. Alam clarified that there is no evidence at this point linking the sibling directly to the crime. Based on initial CCTV footage, police believe the attack may not have been meticulously planned. “‘Yung mga galawan ng mga suspects, parang hindi naman siya ganun kaplanado kasi parang nasa mga 20s lang ‘yung mga suspects. Nagkataon lang talaga, parang kung sino ‘yung may opportunity, ‘yun ang papasukin nila,” Alam said. Alam said there was no indication that Carpenter resisted the intruders. Police are also looking into the possibility that the suspects were under the influence of illegal drugs or alcohol at the time of the attack. “For the moment, naikita namin is purely intent to gain. As claimed by the surviving victim po, mayroon P50,000 cash [na kinuha], plus another cash doon sa wallet nung victim na may laman din P25,000. Tapos isang laptop at saka isang binocular,” Alam said. CARPENTER'S WORK Authorities have found no indication yet that the killing was connected to Carpenter's work as a marine biologist, although investigators continue to examine all possible angles, including his professional activities. The Negros Oriental Police said it has coordinated with the US Embassy regarding the case. Meanwhile, the police’s cybercrime unit is enhancing CCTV footage recovered from the area to help identify the suspects. Investigators hope the improved footage will lead to witnesses who can identify those involved in the killing. RELATED VIDEO

saved_articles.text: American marine biologist Dr. Kent Carpenter. Courtesy: Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park and World Heritage Site MANILA — The Philippine National Police (PNP) has identified another suspect allegedly involved in the killing of American marine biologist Dr. Kent Carpenter, bringing the total number of suspects in the case to six. READ: Police identify 5th suspect in killing of American marine biologist PNP Public Information Office chief PCol. Allen Rae Co said investigators have identified the brother of still at large suspect alias "Eden" as among those allegedly involved in the fatal shooting of Carpenter inside his residence in Sibulan, Negros Oriental. "We now have six suspects actually. 'Yung nauna pong dalawang nahuli, dalawang sumurrender, and then 'yung alyas 'Eden' and his brother, lumalabas po na kasama rin ito," Co said. Police said they are still determining the specific participation of the newly identified suspect, stressing that the investigation remains ongoing and that authorities continue to verify if other individuals were involved. The four suspects already under police custody have undergone inquest proceedings, while charges against the two fugitives will be filed before the prosecutor's office through regular filing. READ: Fourth suspect in American scientist’s slay surrenders Despite the additional suspect, the PNP maintained that robbery remains the primary motive behind the killing. "Wala pa tayong nakikitang to indicate otherwise. Maybe you are talking about the connection sa work niya, wala pa tayong nakikitang ganyan. Although, lahat nga tinitingnan natin. Hindi pa po tapos ito,” Co said. "It doesn't mean that we have identified [the suspects], we have filed cases, e tapos na po ito. We will continue investigating," he added. Police have yet to receive the results of the comprehensive rape examination conducted on Carpenter's live-in partner, who survived the attack. The samples are currently being examined by the PNP Crime Laboratory. The PNP considers the case "solved" under its operational standards, citing the arrest of more than one suspect allegedly involved in the crime, even as efforts continue to locate the two remaining fugitives and determine the possible involvement of other individuals. Courtesy: Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park and World Heritage Site MANILA — Retired Supreme Court associate justice Francis Jardeleza, who served as the Philippines' solicitor general and principal agent in the landmark South China Sea arbitration against China, paid tribute Wednesday to slain American marine biologist Dr. Kent Carpenter , describing him as one of the experts who helped the country secure its historic legal victory. "We, the participants in the Philippine effort to win the Phil v China arbitral award of 2016, deeply mourn the untimely passing of Dr. Kent Carpenter," Jardeleza said in a statement. "He was one of our experts whom we presented in the arbitration, and he did his fair share in espousing our cause. Dr. Kent is a good person, and a very accomplished environmentalist. We pray he rests in peace." Carpenter, 73, was one of two expert witnesses presented by the Philippines during the arbitration proceedings before the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague. As an expert witness, he submitted reports and testified on the condition of coral reef ecosystems in the South China Sea and the environmental damage caused by destructive fishing practices and large-scale activities in the disputed waters. His scientific expertise formed part of the Philippines' evidence in the case that culminated in the landmark July 12, 2016 arbitral award. The tribunal ultimately ruled in favor of the Philippines on several key issues, affirming the country's sovereign rights within its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and finding that China had violated its obligations under international law by causing severe harm to the marine environment through large-scale land reclamation and its failure to prevent Chinese fishermen from harvesting endangered species and damaging fragile coral reef ecosystems. Carpenter, an internationally recognized marine biologist, spent decades studying Philippine marine biodiversity and was widely known for his research on coral reef ecosystems and fish diversity. The tribute came as the Philippine National Police continued its investigation into Carpenter's killing at his home in Sibulan, Negros Oriental. Negros Oriental police chief PCol. Timmar Alam said investigators have identified Carpenter's 34-year-old Filipina live-in partner and her sibling as persons of interest in the case . Police clarified that the designation did not imply criminal liability and that investigators were still validating information gathered during the probe. Authorities said all possible motives remained under investigation. While robbery is among the angles being pursued after cash and personal belongings were reportedly taken from the residence, investigators are also looking into whether the killing could have been connected to Carpenter's professional work, business interests, or personal life. The Philippine National Police has formed a Special Investigation Task Group to fast-track the investigation through forensic examination, intelligence gathering, witness interviews and CCTV review. Initial police investigation showed that on Sunday evening, three unidentified men wearing bonnets forced their way into Carpenter's residence in Barangay Ajong while he and his live-in partner were watching television. One of the suspects allegedly shot Carpenter in the head, killing him at the scene. His partner was reportedly tied up and sustained minor injuries before the suspects fled with cash and other personal belongings. Carpenter had been working in the Philippines since 1975, dedicating much of his career to the study and conservation of the country's marine ecosystems. Beyond his contribution as one of the Philippines' expert witnesses in the landmark South China Sea arbitration, he authored the landmark scientific paper that identified the Verde Island Passage as the world's "Center of the Center of Marine Shore Fish Biodiversity," underscoring the region's extraordinary marine richness. Carpenter also served as an adjunct professor and associate researcher at Silliman University, where he mentored generations of Filipino marine scientists and advanced marine conservation research. Scientific community grieves, demands justice for slain marine expert The Negros Oriental Police Provincial Office has identified the fifth suspect in the robbery and killing of 76-year-old American marine biologist Dr. Kent Carpenter in Barangay Ajong, Sibulan, Negros Oriental, on the night of July 12. Police Captain Stephen Jaynard Polinar, spokesperson of the Negros Oriental Police Provincial Office and the Special Investigation Task Group (SITG) Carpenter, said a 26-year-old alleged gunman and his 40-year-old accomplice were arrested on the night of July 15. The 40-year-old suspect was also accused of sexually assaulting Carpenter's 34-year-old live-in partner. Partner of slain US marine biologist now among 'persons of interest' “As per her account, sir, meron naman daw talaga, ni-rape daw po talaga siya. So, hindi naman natin, we cannot exclude yung fact na yun, sir kasi it's a crime against her honor, no? So, yun, sir, yung nangyari dun, sir,” said Polinar. “She undergone physical and medical examination and we submitted ‘yong mga sample, ‘yong mga nakuha nating evidence for DNA testing sa ating crime laboratory… To back it up lang talaga doon sa account niya na may nangyari sa kanya, sir.” Polinar said the 40-year-old suspect previously worked for Carpenter during the renovation of his house in 2023. Another 21-year-old suspect, who allegedly served as a lookout, surrendered to authorities in the early hours of July 16. Later on the same day, another 21-year-old man also tagged as a lookout surrendered. “Based on our background investigation, some of them have been previously charged with offense. May record na sila ng kaso, sir. Lahat sila, sir,” Polinar added. Authorities said the suspects allegedly took more than P100,000 worth of cash and valuables from the victims. Fourth suspect in American scientist’s slay surrenders “May nakuhang P50,000 na cash sa isang drawer sir and then doon po sa bag ng victim sir may nakukang mga wallet, cash around P25,000 pesos, ATMs and then identification cards and then a laptop sir.” Authorities have filed robbery with homicide charges against the suspects. Police are continuing their investigation into the motive behind Carpenter's killing. Initial investigation, however, indicated that the suspects had targeted the victims' home for robbery. Courtesy: Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park and World Heritage Site MANILA — A fourth suspect in the killing of American marine biologist Dr. Kent Carpenter in Negros Oriental surrendered to authorities on Friday. PNP Public Information Office chief PCol. Allen Rae Co said the suspect, who allegedly served as another lookout during the crime, turned himself in to police in the Police Regional Office–Negros Island Region (PRO-NIR). “Merong bagong lumabas na isang tao na lookout din daw siya. Siguro na-guilty siya kasi diba ang initial natin ay 4 lamang sila so siguro gusto niya rin maglabas ‘yung partisipasyon niya sa krimen,” Co said. According to Co, the latest surrender corroborated the earlier statement of another suspect that there were actually two lookouts assigned during the attack. “Hindi malalaman nung live-in partner dahil nasa loob lang sila ng bahay. Hindi niya alam actually kung sino or meron bang lookout. So lumalabas dalawa ang lookout as of now,” he added. The surrender came a day after authorities announced the arrest of three other suspects: the alleged gunman, the suspect accused of sexually assaulting Carpenter's live-in partner, and another lookout who also voluntarily surrendered. Police are still searching for another suspect identified by alias "Eden." “We are still looking for one. Again, humihingi kami ng tulong sa mga kababayan na kung merong impormasyon kay alias Eden ay ipagbigay-alam niyo lang kaagad sa pinakamalapit na himpilan ng pulisya,” Co said. Meanwhile, police said Carpenter's live-in partner had undergone a comprehensive rape examination. Authorities are still awaiting the results, while DNA samples have been collected and will be sent to Manila for confirmatory testing. Carpenter, a renowned marine biologist known for his extensive work in documenting and conserving Philippine marine biodiversity , was shot dead inside his home in Sibulan, Negros Oriental on July 12. Ex-Solgen pays tribute to slain scientist who helped PH win South China Sea arbitration During the attack, his live-in partner was allegedly sexually assaulted by one of the suspects. Investigators earlier said robbery appeared to be the primary motive behind the killing, although they continued to pursue all possible angles for further investigation. Scientific community grieves, demands justice for slain marine expert Kent Carpenter MANILA — Tributes and calls for justice continue to pour in following the killing of renowned marine biologist Dr. Kent Carpenter, who was found dead inside his home in Sibulan, Negros Oriental on Sunday. Scientists, environmental groups, and conservation advocates are mourning the loss of a researcher whose decades of work helped transform the understanding and protection of the Philippines' rich marine biodiversity. Greenpeace Philippines described Carpenter's death as a significant loss at a time when the country's seas are increasingly threatened by climate change, plastic pollution, and biodiversity loss. "At a time when the worsening plastic and climate crises continue to threaten our seas and the communities that depend on them, we need more people like Dr. Kent who champion the protection of our environment and stand with communities," the group said. Carpenter's connection to the Philippines began in the 1970s after earning his biology degree. Assigned by the Peace Corps to work as a researcher with the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), he later described the assignment as the best job he had during his Peace Corps service. Partner of slain US marine biologist now among 'persons of interest' His work in the country led him to collaborate with National Scientist Dr. Angel Alcala, one of the pioneers of marine conservation in the Philippines. Their partnership helped shape decades of research on coral reefs, reef fishes, and marine ecosystems. Carpenter also developed close ties with Silliman University, where he mentored Filipino scientists and opened opportunities for local researchers to collaborate with international institutions. Dr. Robert Guino-o of Silliman University, who considered Carpenter his mentor, remembered him not only for his scientific expertise but also for his compassion toward students and coastal communities. ”I remember he would sit down and take the time to listen to concerns ranging from research or personal concerns before he would give his advice," Guino-o said. "He will be sorely missed talaga sa Silliman and certainly a big loss to the scientific community. He has this care for students, fisherfolks, fish vendors. He's good at Tagalog and a bit of Cebuano. These are traits that really endeared him to many people.” The University of the Philippines Marine Science Institute also paid tribute to Carpenter, highlighting his pioneering studies on Philippine coral reefs, reef fishes, and fisheries that laid the foundation for modern coral reef ecology in the country. According to the institute, Carpenter's research helped establish the Philippines as the "center of the center of marine shore fish biodiversity," a global recognition of the country's unparalleled diversity of reef fishes. He also strongly advocated for the protection of the Verde Island Passage, one of the world's most biologically diverse marine ecosystems, pushing for its designation as a National Protected Area and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Beyond marine biodiversity research, Carpenter also played a key role in the Philippines' arbitration case against China over the West Philippine Sea. As one of the country's scientific advisers, he contributed expert reports, testimony, satellite imagery, and video evidence documenting the condition of coral reefs damaged by large-scale activities in disputed waters. Environmental groups said Carpenter's legacy extended far beyond scientific publications. American marine biologist gunned down in Negros Oriental, partner assaulted The Kalikasan People's Network described his killing as an attack not only on environmental defenders but also on the communities that have benefited from his decades of work in marine conservation. "Hindi lang sa mga environmental defenders sa Pilipinas, kundi pati sa mga komunidad. Kailangan natin siguraduhin yung mga pinagdaanan ni Dr. Kent ay mabibigyan ng hustisya. Na hindi lang ito mapupunta sa hangin, na hindi lang ito maitatago sa mga library, hindi lang matatago sa mga dokumento, kundi malalaman ito ng mga komunidad," said Kalikasan spokesperson Cathleen de Guzman. In a report on Friday, authorities have apprehended suspects of Carpenter's killing. Still colleagues and advocates are calling for swift justice while honoring a scientist whose life's work helped reveal the extraordinary richness of Philippine marine ecosystems and inspired generations of Filipino researchers dedicated to protecting them.
